stem: A steel wire of length \(4.7\,\text{m}\) and cross-sectional area \(3.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}^2\) stretches by the same amount as a copper wire of length \(3.5\,\text{m}\) and cross-sectional area of \(4.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}^2\) under a given load. What is the ratio of the Young's modulus of steel to that of copper?
Figure 8.9 shows the strain-stress curve for a given material. What are (a) Young's modulus and (b) approximate yield strength for this material?
_note: The book prints "strain-stress curve"; Fig. 8.9 plots Stress on the vertical axis against Strain on the horizontal axis, i.e. what is conventionally called a stress-strain curve. Transcribed as printed. The (a)/(b) here are two quantities asked inside one interrogative sentence, not separate printed sub-items, so this ships as a single question.

stem:
The stress-strain graphs for materials \(A\) and \(B\) are shown in Fig. 8.10. The graphs are drawn to the same scale.

(a) Which of the materials has the greater Young's modulus?

The stress-strain graphs for materials \(A\) and \(B\) are shown in Fig. 8.10. The graphs are drawn to the same scale.

(b) Which of the two is the stronger material?

Read the following statement below carefully and state, with reasons, if it is true or false.

(a) The Young's modulus of rubber is greater than that of steel;

Read the following statement below carefully and state, with reasons, if it is true or false.

(b) The stretching of a coil is determined by its shear modulus.

Two wires of diameter \(0.25\,\text{cm}\), one made of steel and the other made of brass are loaded as shown in Fig. 8.11. The unloaded length of steel wire is \(1.5\,\text{m}\) and that of brass wire is \(1.0\,\text{m}\). Compute the elongations of the steel and the brass wires.
_note: Unanswerable from the stem alone: the two loads (\(4.0\,\text{kg}\) hung at the steel-brass junction and \(6.0\,\text{kg}\) at the lower end) are printed ONLY in Fig. 8.11 and appear nowhere in the text. The figure is required.

stem: The edge of an aluminium cube is \(10\,\text{cm}\) long. One face of the cube is firmly fixed to a vertical wall. A mass of \(100\,\text{kg}\) is then attached to the opposite face of the cube. The shear modulus of aluminium is \(25\,\text{GPa}\). What is the vertical deflection of this face?

Four identical hollow cylindrical columns of mild steel support a big structure of mass \(50{,}000\,\text{kg}\). The inner and outer radii of each column are \(30\) and \(60\,\text{cm}\) respectively. Assuming the load distribution to be uniform, calculate the compressional strain of each column.

A piece of copper having a rectangular cross-section of \(15.2\,\text{mm} \times 19.1\,\text{mm}\) is pulled in tension with \(44{,}500\,\text{N}\) force, producing only elastic deformation. Calculate the resulting strain?

A steel cable with a radius of \(1.5\,\text{cm}\) supports a chairlift at a ski area. If the maximum stress is not to exceed \(10^{8}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\), what is the maximum load the cable can support?

A rigid bar of mass \(15\,\text{kg}\) is supported symmetrically by three wires each \(2.0\,\text{m}\) long. Those at each end are of copper and the middle one is of iron. Determine the ratios of their diameters if each is to have the same tension.

A \(14.5\,\text{kg}\) mass, fastened to the end of a steel wire of unstretched length \(1.0\,\text{m}\), is whirled in a vertical circle with an angular velocity of \(2\,\text{rev/s}\) at the bottom of the circle. The cross-sectional area of the wire is \(0.065\,\text{cm}^2\). Calculate the elongation of the wire when the mass is at the lowest point of its path.

Compute the bulk modulus of water from the following data: Initial volume \(= 100.0\,\text{litre}\), Pressure increase \(= 100.0\,\text{atm}\) \((1\,\text{atm} = 1.013 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa})\), Final volume \(= 100.5\,\text{litre}\). Compare the bulk modulus of water with that of air (at constant temperature). Explain in simple terms why the ratio is so large.
What is the density of water at a depth where pressure is \(80.0\,\text{atm}\), given that its density at the surface is \(1.03 \times 103\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\)?
_note: PRINTED DEFECT, transcribed faithfully — this is NOT a transcription slip on our side. The book prints the surface density as "1.03 x 103 kg m^-3" with the exponent of ten set on the BASELINE (flat "103"), while the "m^-3" beside it in the same line is correctly superscripted, and 8.12 and 8.15 on the same page correctly print \(10^{5}\) and \(10^{6}\) — so the flattening is a one-off typesetting fault on this item, not a page-wide rendering artefact. Verified at 5x zoom. The physically intended value is \(1.03 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\) (the density of sea water); as printed, \(103\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\) is about a tenth of water's density and the question would be unanswerable. Flagged for the answer-key cross-check to adjudicate.

stem: Compute the fractional change in volume of a glass slab, when subjected to a hydraulic pressure of \(10\,\text{atm}\).
Determine the volume contraction of a solid copper cube, \(10\,\text{cm}\) on an edge, when subjected to a hydraulic pressure of \(7.0 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Pa}\).
How much should the pressure on a litre of water be changed to compress it by \(0.10\%\)?
_note: PRINTED DEFECT — orphaned text. Item 8.16 is followed on its own second line by the stray fragment "carry one quarter of the load." (verified at 5x zoom), which is a sentence tail belonging to no question: it does not parse with 8.16, and 8.16 itself is complete and answerable as it ends at "0.10%?". It reads as the surviving tail of a question deleted in the rationalised edition (cf. 8.7, whose four columns each carry one quarter of a load). The fragment is recorded verbatim here rather than in the stem, so nothing is lost but the shipped question stays answerable. This is the LAST item of the chapter's EXERCISES block; the remainder of the page is blank.
